1Introduction

Purpose. This page is groundwork for a project to improve bird-sound recognition for the species and biomes that current models serve poorly. It is not a leaderboard. Its job is to describe where three widely used models stand today, measured carefully enough that a later improvement can be told apart from noise.

Improving on existing models starts with understanding them. The leading models share a broad approach: they turn audio into a spectrogram and score every species they know. They differ in many design decisions: how long a window they listen to, the sample rate, the training data, the label set and the scale of their output.

Running and comparing them fairly is harder than it looks. Species names have to be mapped onto one taxonomy, scores put on a common footing, and each model's windows matched to labels that were drawn on a different grid. Methods (section 2) explains how each of these is handled.

The page is organised around four aims:

  1. Replicate published results before proposing any improvement.
  2. Understand how the models work and where they differ mechanically.
  3. Define the evaluation criteria, and why each matters for passive soundscape monitoring, where a wrong detection costs more than a missed one.
  4. Establish a baseline by site, biome and species, and find where performance is weakest.

What we found.

  • Replication. Perch V2 reproduces 21 of 21 published per-site values within 0.02 (3.1).
  • Weakest areas. Performance is weakest in tropical moist forest, where mean per-species AP is 0.31–0.44 across models against 0.39–0.74 in the other biomes. It is also weaker for species with few xeno-canto recordings and for species with few labelled examples (3.3).
  • Mechanics change conclusions. Perch's raw scores sit at different levels for different species, so a single deployment threshold serves it badly even though it ranks recordings well: its recording-level cmAP is 0.680, close to BirdNET's 0.701 and 0.735, but its recall at 90% precision is 0.350 against 0.506 and 0.509 (3.2).

How to read this page. Methods (section 2) covers the data, the models, the pipeline and the metrics. Results 3.4 holds the species tables: per-species metrics, traits, calling times, call frequencies and links to xeno-canto, eBird and the Macaulay Library for each species at each site.

BirdNET may have been trained on recordings from these test sites, so its results here may be optimistic (2.3).

2Methods

2.1From sound to prediction

A model never hears a whole recording at once. It listens to a fixed window of audio, a few seconds long, turns it into a spectrogram (a picture of sound energy across time and frequency) and returns a score for every species it knows. Sliding the window along the recording gives a score for each species in each window.

The evaluation then turns those window scores into claims about two things: which species are present in each labelled 5-second segment, and which species are present in each recording. The figure shows one excerpt. BirdNET and Perch slice the same audio differently: BirdNET into 3-second windows, Perch into 5-second windows.

2.2Dataset: BirdSet

BirdSet (Rauch et al. 2025, ICLR 2025, arXiv:2403.10380) is a benchmark for bird-sound classification. Its training set, XCL, holds 528,434 xeno-canto recordings of 9,734 classes; its test data are eight soundscape datasets annotated by experts, more than 400 hours in all (published figures). Here every test site is scored: 1,723 recordings, 447 hours.

  • POW is BirdSet's validation set, not a test set. It is included here like the others.
  • NBP is not a soundscape set. Its “recordings” are clips of a few seconds each, so its recording-level results mean little.
  • Most sites record only around dawn. SSW records around the clock and UHH from early morning to late evening, so only those two show full daily patterns. BirdSet gives PER's and SSW's times in UTC (their file names end in Z); they are converted to local time (scripts/site_calls.py). NBP has no clock times or frequency boxes.
  • Site biomes are WWF biomes assigned per site (configs/reference/sites.csv). The sites are small areas, so a label describes the site's setting, not every recorder.

Label check. Before relying on BirdSet's 5-second labels, they were rebuilt from its call-level annotations (a call counts for a segment when it overlaps it by at least 0.5 s) and compared with the official labels, from metadata alone (scripts/birdset_labels.py). They agree exactly on 96% to 100% of segments at 7 sites (100% at POW), and on 52% at NBP.

Two modes. Clips mode follows BirdSet's protocol: each site's 5-second test clips, every species in the site's label set. It is the mode that can be compared with published figures. Soundscape mode runs the models over the full recordings, as a deployment would, and scores each 5-second segment and each recording. Both are reported because they answer different questions: does the harness reproduce the literature, and how would the models do on the recordings a monitoring project collects.

Species information. To ask which kinds of species are served poorly, each species is described from outside sources: body mass, lifestyle and habitat from AVONET; diet, foraging stratum and a nocturnal flag from EltonTraits 1.0, matched to eBird names through AVONET's crosswalk; the number of xeno-canto recordings, queried on 2026-10-11; and, from BirdSet's call annotations, each species' call frequency band and calling times at each site. The xeno-canto counts are today's counts, larger than what any model trained on, and xeno-canto's IOC names can split or lump species differently from eBird's. These sources are how “underrepresented” is measured in 3.3.

2.3Models: shared approach, different decisions

All three models take a mono waveform, compute a spectrogram inside the model, and return a score per class per window. Everything else differs, and several of the differences matter for this project:

Perch V2 is loaded through the birdnet Python package (version 1.1.1), which downloads a converted copy of the model. The replication in 3.1 shows that it behaves like the published model.

Training-data overlap. BirdSet left BirdNET out of its comparisons “due to potential test data leakage” (Rauch et al. 2025, section 4.1): BirdNET may have been trained on recordings from these sites. Overlap has not been checked for any model here, so BirdNET's results in particular may be optimistic.

2.4Running the models side by side

Comparing the models fairly took four decisions:

  • One package for all three. BirdNET 2.4, BirdNET 3.0 and Perch V2 all run through the birdnet package, with the same audio loading and the same window settings per model.
  • One label space. Every model's labels are mapped to scientific names in the 2025 eBird taxonomy, through eBird codes and configs/taxonomy/synonyms.yaml for names that changed. Every species at every site is scored for every model, including the 4 species BirdNET 2.4 cannot predict (at NBP, NES), which count against it.
  • Raw logits, cached before any scoring decision. Each model's raw output is stored per file, so every later choice (score scale, alignment, metric) is applied to the same predictions.
  • One alignment rule for matching model windows to labelled segments, set out below.

Design decision: the alignment rule

Model windows and BirdSet's 5-second segments lie on different grids, so each window has to be assigned to a segment. Under the first rule tried, any window overlapping a segment by at least 1 second counted for it. Perch's 5-second windows then scored calls in the neighbouring segment: on POW its soundscape cmAP was 0.471 against 0.567 on clips (historical numbers, under the old rule, from decision_point.md).

The rule now used is the half-window rule: a window counts for the segment that holds more than half of it. It follows from the window geometry alone and was not tuned on results. Perch on POW now scores 0.557 on clips and 0.542 in the soundscapes.

Three class scopes. Each result can be computed over all of a site's species (all), over the species a given model can predict (covered), or over the species every model can predict (shared). This page uses all, BirdSet's protocol, unless stated.

Three-state labels. A species is present, absent, or not reviewed in each segment. Audio that nobody reviewed is left out of every metric rather than counted as absent.

2.5Evaluation criteria

Each metric answers a different question, and each matters here for a different reason.

cmAP (primary)
Average precision per species, averaged over species. Because each species counts once, rare and underrepresented species weigh as much as common ones, which is the point of this project.
AUROC
The chance that a segment with the species scores higher than one without it, averaged over species. It does not depend on how common a species is, so it compares fairly across sites and hours.
Top-1
The share of segments with at least one label where the top-scoring species is one of them. Reported for comparability with BirdSet.
Recording-level presence
The deployment question: is species X in this recording? Recording cmAP is cmAP over recordings instead of segments. Recall at 80, 90 and 95% precision is the share of true presences found at the single score threshold where that share of claims is right. List precision is the share of a recording's claimed species that are really there. In clips mode each clip is its own recording.
Evidence precision
A detection is only useful if a person can check it. For each species claimed at the 90%-precision threshold, the model cites its highest-scoring window as evidence; the evidence is right when that window overlaps an annotated call of the species by at least 0.5 s. The conditional version counts only claims that are right at recording level, separating “wrong species” from “right species, wrong clip”.

Uncertainty. Intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals that resample whole recordings, because segments within a recording are correlated: resampling segments would make the intervals too narrow.

Per-species reporting. A group mean can hide species that fail completely, so results are also given per species (3.3 and 3.4). Per-species AP is noisy for species with only a few labelled segments; group means pool many species, but their intervals still widen as groups get small.

3Results

3.1Replication

Before measuring anything new, the harness has to reproduce what has been published. Perch V2 in clips mode is compared with the three Perch 2.0 variants in van Merriënboer et al. 2025 (arXiv:2508.04665, Appendix C, Table 4). A value counts as within when it is no more than 0.02 outside the published range. 21 of 21 values on 7 sites are within; none falls more than 0.008 below the published range.

Taxonomy mapping matters at this level of agreement: before the current configs/taxonomy/synonyms.yaml, Perch was 0.01–0.02 below the published cmAP and AUROC on HSN and SNE (historical numbers).

3.2Overall baseline

Segment cmAP per site in clips mode, with 95% intervals over recordings. This is the starting point any improvement will be measured against.

  • Site difficulty. PER (Amazon Basin) is the hardest site for 2 of 3 models, at 0.23–0.38 cmAP: it has 132 species and about 37 species per recording, far more than any other site.
  • Recording level depends on each model's score scale. Averaged over the 8 soundscape sites, recording-level cmAP is 0.701 for BirdNET 2.4, 0.735 for BirdNET 3.0 and 0.680 for Perch V2: the models rank recordings similarly well. Recall at 90% precision, which needs one threshold to work for every species, is 0.506, 0.509 and 0.350. Perch's logits run high for every species and at different levels per species, so a single threshold that keeps its precision at 90% must sit high enough to miss many presences.
  • Evidence precision. At that threshold, the window a model cites as evidence holds the claimed species for 79% (BirdNET 2.4), 77% (BirdNET 3.0) and 78% (Perch V2) of claims, mean over sites. Among claims that are right at recording level, it is 87%, 85% and 87%: even when the species is right, some cited clips would not let a listener confirm it.

3.3Where performance is weakest

“Underrepresented” has two meanings here, and they are kept apart. Training representation (how many xeno-canto recordings a species has; which region and biome it lives in) is what the project aims to change. Test prevalence (how many labelled segments a species has at a site) mostly limits how precisely its performance can be measured.

  • Biome. Tropical moist broadleaf forest (NES, PER, UHH; 248 site–species pairs) has mean per-species AP of 0.31–0.44 across models, the lowest biome for 3 of 3 models. Temperate conifer forest (HSN, SNE) is at 0.39–0.47, temperate broadleaf and mixed forest (POW, SSW) at 0.47–0.64, and the Mediterranean site (NBP; 51 pairs) at 0.51–0.74. With one to three sites per biome, a biome's result is largely its sites' results.
  • Xeno-canto recordings. Species with under 100 xeno-canto recordings (63 pairs) average 0.30–0.44 AP across models, against 0.50–0.66 for species with 2,000 or more (34 pairs). The gap is smallest for BirdNET 2.4 (0.444 against 0.497) and largest for BirdNET 3.0 (0.348 against 0.658). 81 pairs have no xeno-canto count yet.
  • Labelled examples. Species with 1–9 labelled segments average 0.29–0.38 AP across models, 10–49 segments 0.36–0.45, and 50 or more 0.48–0.58. Part of this gap is measurement: AP from a handful of positives is noisy.

Each of these claims rests on groups of at least ten site–species pairs. The explorer's Groups view shows these and other groupings (habitat, body mass, diet, call frequency) with intervals, for every site or one at a time.

The weakest species. A fixed rule, set before looking at the result: in clips mode, among the (site, species) pairs with at least 10 labelled segments, the 20 with the lowest best AP over the three models. A low value means every model struggles with that species at that site. 10 of the 20 are at PER, and no model reaches AP 0.11 on any of them.

3.4Species-level data and the explorer

The explorer holds every result above at finer grain. Choose clips or soundscapes and one site or all of them, then a view:

  • Overview: each model at each site, with the best value per site in bold.
  • Groups: mean per-species AP by trait, biome, prevalence, call frequency or xeno-canto count.
  • Species: one row per site and species. Pick the metric, compare two models in the difference column, search by name, family or habitat, hide species with fewer than ten positives, and add trait columns. Click a name for its traits, calling times by local hour, call frequency band, and links to xeno-canto, eBird and the Macaulay Library. Calling activity is calls per recorded hour; hours a site never recorded are shown as unknown.
  • Hours: bird activity and model performance by local hour of day, from the soundscapes.

4Conclusion

What the groundwork establishes.

  • The harness reproduces published Perch results: 21 of 21 per-site values within 0.02. Results measured with it can be set beside the literature.
  • Model mechanics shape comparisons. Window length decides which calls a window can hear and which segment it counts for; score scales decide how well one threshold works across species; label spaces decide which species a model can be scored on at all.
  • The baseline has clear gaps: tropical sites (0.31–0.44 mean AP), species with little xeno-canto audio (0.30–0.44 for those under 100 recordings), and the 20 weakest species in 3.3.

Next steps that the repository already points to:

  • Per-species calibration of presence confidence, so one target precision can be met with a threshold per species rather than one for all (Phase 5 of the recording-level evaluation design).
  • Geographic filtering, available for both BirdNET versions in the birdnet package and not used here.
  • Expert listening of the highest-scoring false positives, which each run lists in fp_review.csv, to learn how many are missed labels rather than model errors.
  • Further checks on training-data overlap between each model and the BirdSet test sites.

Limitations.

  • BirdNET may have been trained on recordings from these test sites, so its results may be optimistic.
  • BirdNET 3.0 is a developer preview; its models and labels will change.
  • There are 8 sites, one to three per biome, so a biome's result is largely its sites' results.
  • Xeno-canto counts are current counts, not counts as of any model's training.
  • No geographic filtering is applied.
  • BirdSet's labels are assumed exhaustive: a species calling but not annotated counts as a false positive.

Reproduce this

Everything on this page is generated from the repository. From a checkout:

uv pip install -e ".[models,perch,birdset,report,dev]"

# clips mode (BirdSet's protocol) and soundscape mode, one site at a time
for s in HSN NBP NES PER POW SNE SSW UHH; do
  birdeval run -m birdnet_2.4 birdnet_3.0 perch_v2 -e birdset_$s --run-name full_$s
  birdeval run -m birdnet_2.4 birdnet_3.0 perch_v2 -e birdset_${s}_scape --run-name full_${s}_scape
done

python -I scripts/build_report.py results/full_*      # report tables -> results/report/
python -I scripts/hourly.py                            # by hour of day, from the cached predictions
python -I scripts/fig_spectrogram.py                   # the figure in 2.1
python -I scripts/render_report.py                     # this page -> docs/index.html

Predictions are cached per file, so an interrupted run resumes where it stopped, and rebuilding the tables or the page never re-runs a model. This page was rendered on 2026-10-12 from repository version 2f6b742-dirty with the birdnet package 1.1.1. The prose lives in report/sections and its numbers come from the tables through scripts/report_content.py.
